newsitem.title: USA: U.S. paper capacity growth set to slow - survey.
newsitem.headline: U.S. paper capacity growth set to slow - survey.

text.p: U.S. pulp, paper and paperboard capacity will grow at less than historical rates over the next three years, according to an industry trade association.
Paper and paperboard capacity is expected to grow at a 1.5 percent average annual rate during the next three years, the American Forest & Paper Association's capacity survey found.

It rose 3.5 percent in 1996 and an average of 2.6 percent from 1986 to 1995, the group said. On a tonnage basis, capacity was expected to rise from 99.1 million tons in 1996 to 103.7 million tons in 1999, it said.
More than half of the anticipated capacity expansions would be due to improved efficiency from existing machines, the survey said.

"The industry's heavy reliance on improving the productivity of existing machines demonstrates its prudent use of limited investment dollars," Richard Storat, the association's president for policy research, said.
Consumption of recovered paper would continue to expand at a more rapid pace than paper and paperboard capacity, the association said.
U.S. mill consumption of recovered paper rose 9.2 percent in 1996 and was expected to grow 2.9 percent in the 1997 through 1999 period, the association said.
Market wood pulp capacity, which fell 1.4 percent in 1996 to 11 million tons, was expected to remain stable during the next three years, the survey said.
But recovered market pulp capacity was expected to continue to show strong gains, registering average annual growth of 12.6 percent during the next the next years from a small base, the survey said.
Paper capacity is expected to rise at an annual rate of 1.3 percent during 1997 to 1999, compared to average annual growth of 2.2 percent from 1986 to 1995 and 1.7 percent in 1996, the survey said.

Capacity growth would range below historical norms for newsprint and printing-writing papers during the next three years, while tissue paper capacity growth was projected to match historical norms, the survey said.
Paper and industrial converting paper capacity was set to expand modestly, it said.
Paperboard capacity was expected to increase an average 1.7 percent annually during the next three years, from 51.6 million tons in 1996 to 54.3 million tons in 1999.

Boxboard capacity was expected to record average annual growth of 2.3 percent through 1999 while containerboard was expected to register annual capacity growth of 1.7 percent during the next three years, the survey said.

Wood pulp capacity would increase just 0.6 percent annually fron 1997 to 1999, to 70.7 million tons, the survey said. Recovered paper market pulp capacity would show strong growth, rising from 1.4 million tons in 1996 to almost two million tons in 1999, it said.
